## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.54139.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.54139.sa1)

In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

A new paper by Jerjian et al. provides the most thorough investigation of the population activity during grasp execution and observation in primary motor cortex (M1) and premotor cortex (F5) to date. Modulation of activity during action observation was observed in pyramidal tract neurons in both F5 and M1. The neuronal state in M1 during observation, however, was much more similar to a condition in which the monkey needed to withhold a response. This sheds new light onto the way the motor system prevents observation-related activity from causing overt movements.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Movement initiation and grasp representation in premotor and primary motor cortex mirror neurons" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, including Jörn Diedrichsen as the Reviewing Editor and Reviewer #1, and the evaluation has been overseen by Floris de Lange as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Luca Bonini (Reviewer #2).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

This manuscript provides new and interesting evidence about the way in which primates' motor system can code executed and observed actions without invariably turn the latter into an unwanted motor output. Even pyramidal tract neurons can code observed actions, as previously demonstrated by different groups. The population-based analysis of execution, observation, and withholding related activity in M1 and PMd provides new insights into the role of these two areas as crucial nodes in the action observation network. Specifically M1 may dissociate abstract signals about (observed or withheld) grasp representations from executive, descending signals required for actively performing the movement.

Essential revisions:

1) There was some initial uncertainty about what aspect of the paper actually provided a novel insights. The orthogonal subspaces in M1 for execution and observation, and the stronger observation activity in PMd are nice to show empirically, but not necessarily new or unexpected. Ultimately, all reviewers were under the impression that the paper could provide support for the idea that the neural dynamics occurring during withheld actions (in no-go condition) also happen during action observation in M1, but not in F5. This mechanism would make it possible for F5 to represent observed actions with a net facilitation, which is not turned into an unwanted motor output because M1 behaves like during no-go trials. This idea, however, was not very clearly spelled out in the paper and would need much more explaining (see reviewer 1 comment 2, reviewer 2 comment 1, reviewer 3 comments 3-4). Are there alternative interpretations for a similarity of No-go and observation trials in M1? Can the activity be more conclusively shown to be related to withholding?

2) It is not clear why the analysis was split by grasp-type. See reviewer 1 comment 1 and reviewer 2 comment 4. Would it be not informative to analyze whether the observation of an action is similar to the execution of the same action (as compared to another one)? While one may not expect to find a strict visuomotor congruence in the motor and visual selectivity (see Bonini et al., 2014 and Papadourakis and Raos, 2019), it would be important to show how the current results interact with the factor "object"– i.e. comparing the selectivity of grasp representations during execution and observation. At the very least, a combined analysis would hopefully simplify and streamline the result presentation.

3) Finally, many methodological choices (normalization, etc) are not very well justified. The original reviews are appended below and the authors should carefully clarify why the current methods are used.

Reviewer #1:

The paper provides a thorough analysis of mirror-like activity in area F5 and M1 during the execution of two grasp types (precision and whole hand). An additional strength of the paper is the actual identification of M1- PTN neurons. The main conclusions are that F5 shows a correspondence between observation and execution activity, whereas in M1-PTN and M1-UID units, the activity is evolving in relatively independent subspaces.

This alone may explain how the monkey can prevent overt EMG from being generated in the observe conditions. The interpretation of the additional no-go condition in this study is less clear (see point 2).

1) I believe that the paper certainly goes beyond current papers on mirror neuron activity. However, it was not 100% clear what novel conclusions can be really drawn from the paper. Specifically, I was left wondering why the authors conducted the analyses separately for each grasp type. One of the key questions I think is to what degree the difference between neural trajectories that distinguish different types of grasp are re-visited in observation. The current analyses make it impossible to discern whether units that fire more for precision than whole-hand grasp during execution also do so during observations. I think the interesting claim to test is whether observation and execution involve the same action codes. Right now communalities can be driven simply by common variations across the trial time course.

2) The section "movement suppression during action observation" is not clearly motivated. Knowing that there is subspace overlap between No-go and observation activity does per se tell us anything about movement suppression, or does it? These ideas are not spelled out clearer in the Discussion. What are "suppression-like features of the unfolding action observation response in M1"?

Reviewer #2:

This manuscript provides new and interesting evidence about the way in which primates' motor system can code executed and observed actions without invariably turn the latter into an unwanted motor output. Indeed, primary motor neurons can code observed actions, as previously demonstrated by different groups (including the senior author's group), but their activity is remarkably different from that during execution and much more similar to that during a new NoGo condition in which the monkey is required to withhold the action. The findings provide compelling evidence that the primary motor cortex is a crucial node of the action observation network because it may dissociate abstract signals about (observed or withheld) grasp representations from executive, descending signals required for actively performing the movement.

I found the data novel and interesting, and the paper is, in general, technically sound. I have some doubts about data analysis and some suggestions to improve data presentation.

1) During NoGo trials, "a red LED required the monkey to simply remain on the homepads for the duration of the trial". Fine, but please state what the monkey sees exactly in the different conditions, where the experimenter (hand in particular) was in the meantime, and where he/she was during Go condition.

2) I assume the monkey was not fixating: but was there any control of eye position? If not, it should be discussed or stated in some part of the manuscript whether and why possible systematic differences in gaze/attention allocation during the various conditions (e.g. Maranesi et al., 2013) should or should not have influenced the action observation response.

3) Reward. "The monkey received a small fruit reward directly to the mouth for each successfully completed execution, observation or NoGo trials". Who or what (if any automatic device was used) gave the food to the monkey? When was it delivered relative to the tone indicating the end of the trial? From Figure 1C and single neuron examples I assume the reward delivery is outside the illustrated period, but it would be useful to see the response also during this last phase of the task because it is known that the reward can strongly influence the visual response of mirror neurons, at least in PMv (Caggiano et al. 2012 PNAS). In 2 out of 4 single neuron examples (Figure 4A, D) the activity after HPN does not return to baseline level (in Figure 5 the same problem is apparent), supporting the usefulness of seeing what happens next. It should also be stated if the fruit reward was always the same or if it was varied (and, in case, when).

4) I don't understand why some epochs for single-neuron analyses have been (apparently arbitrarily) split into two: this should be at least justified. Furthermore, I cannot understand why baseline has been used in a post-hoc comparison only: it could be reasonable to treat execution and observation separately, given the often radically different magnitude of activity. But why not using a 2-ways ANOVA (rather than one-way) considering EPOCH (including baseline) and OBJECT as factors?

5) It is not entirely clear from Figure 3 if at least some (if not many) of the penetrations were carried out in the ventro-rostral part of the dorsal premotor cortex (which is known to host mirror neurons as well, see Papadourakis and Raos, 2019): showing the reconstruction of the penetration grid on the cortical surface would help.

Reviewer #3:

The submitted paper by Jerjian and colleagues is a detailed investigation of the relationship between single neuron activity in macaque motor cortex (F5 and M1) and the execution, observation and withholding of reaching/grasping actions.

The experimental setup is straightforward. A monkey sits opposite an experimenter and between them are two reachable objects. An amber LED cues whether the animal or person will potentially manipulate the object (depending on whom it is closer to) and which object will be manipulated (depending on whether it is on the left or right side). The amber LED can then turn either green, cueing an execution of the indicated action or red cueing that the indicated action should not be executed. The basic question now becomes how single neurons and the net populations respond to the various parts of this task. Recordings are done with traditional tools over many sessions yielding populations of 100-200 neurons. Of particular note, the authors identify M1 neurons that project to the corticospinal tract, an important feature of the dataset. They also record from muscles to try and control for the animal's state.

Overall, the paper does a careful job cataloging the findings using several approaches. The writing is clear and for the most part very thorough. The results they report are sensible. F5 maintains a more similar representation of action and observation than does M1. M1 is noted to have evidence of a so-called withholding state which may act to dissociate the representation of the grasp from the execution of an action. My general concern relates to how much this really pushes the field forward as well as some methodological issues with respect to the general approach used how they have handled the EMG analysis.

1) What precisely are the authors doing that is new here? Not being directly in this area, it is hard to tell because I do not see a clear statement of the objectives beyond a desire to investigate this interesting topic more carefully than has previously been done. I do see some interesting things like ensuring that trials are randomized order, having the object in peri-personal space, and recording PTNs. Are these things meant to alter our appreciation of this system? If so, how? It comes across that the authors think it’s obvious but without a specific hypothesis being put forth it all falls a bit flat to me.

2) I know that the authors list the limitations of their approach, but it's worth emphasizing how much insight could potentially be gained here by deploying modern approaches on various scales. A simple one would be looking at single trial activity, hardly a big ask these days even in monkeys. A more exciting one would be looking at causal manipulations. ]

3) What precisely do the authors think constitutes evidence for a withholding state? I can't pin them down on it much more than M1 activity goes down. Again, very nicely demonstrated but not definitive (see EMG point below and note that idea of trial-by-trial recordings are missing) and to some degree loose even in the context of the analysis done as far as I can tell.

4) The details about the EMG are absolutely critical here and yet very much lacking. Is EMG analyzed on the same days as the neural activity? Are the analyses performed on a trial by trial basis? Do the experiments have a handle on whether the muscle activity is above threshold during the various epochs of the task? The authors clearly appreciate that one needs to understand the state of the descending motor signals to make the inferences they want to make but then they provide such a high-level overview that it is hard to understand at what level they appreciate the nuances.

5) I don't understand some arbitrary analytical choices. For example, they eliminate neurons that change activity <5 spikes / second (subsection “Single-neuron analyses”). The smoothing window quite broad and acausal (subsection “Heatmaps and population averages”). They add an offset for rate comparisons of +5 for rate condition comparisons (subsection “Correlation analyses”). I appreciate the clarity of the methods, it’s great, but I would like some further details about these kinds of choices and how they influence the results, especially because these are essentially descriptive.

results.result: Monkeys were trained to high performance (>90% correct) and exhibited significantly faster reaction and movement times than human experimenters. Movement times were 30-50 ms longer for the trapezoid object than the sphere.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 provide behavioral validation of the task. The high performance rate (C32) and statistical comparisons of timing (C33-C34) with appropriate tests (Wilcoxon sign-rank, p<1×10⁻¹³ and p<1×10⁻⁷) demonstrate well-controlled behavioral execution.

results.result: EMG activity during observation and NoGo conditions was negligible and statistically indistinguishable from baseline, while execution showed significant EMG increases.
results.evaluation: Claims C35 and C39 establish critical control data showing no muscle contamination during passive conditions. Statistical tests (t-tests with p<0.00001) and visual inspection (Figure 2) confirm observation and NoGo EMG remained at baseline levels, validating that neural activity during these conditions reflects true mirror/suppression responses rather than subtle movements.

results.result: Repetitive intracortical microstimulation (rICMS) elicited finger/thumb effects at 27/57 M1-PTN sites, 89/124 M1-UID sites, and 75/111 F5 sites. M1 sites predominantly had low thresholds (74-85% ≤20μA) while F5 sites did not (36% ≤20μA).
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C45 provide anatomical validation of recording locations. The rICMS data with specific proportions and threshold measurements confirm recordings were made in hand/finger representations, with expected differences between M1 (low thresholds) and F5 (higher thresholds) consistent with their differential contributions to direct motor control.

results.result: The study recorded 187 M1 neurons (59 PTNs, 128 UIDs) and 115 F5 neurons across two monkeys performing execution, observation, and NoGo conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5 and C46-C47 clearly state the dataset composition. The numbers are internally consistent and provide adequate sample sizes for population-level analyses, with antidromic identification of PTNs providing anatomical specificity.

results.result: During execution, 92.1% of neurons showed epoch effects and 71.5% showed epoch×grasp interactions. During observation, 67.6% showed epoch effects and 19.5% showed interactions. Interaction effects were significantly more frequent during execution (p<0.00001). Overall, 93.4% were modulated during execution, 57.6% during observation, and 56.0% qualified as mirror neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C58 present systematic ANOVA results with appropriate statistics (chi-squared test, p<0.00001). The finding of more frequent grasp-specific interactions during execution than observation is well-supported and provides important characterization of task-related modulation across conditions.

results.result: Facilitation-facilitation mirror neurons showed progressively smaller execution/observation amplitude ratios from M1-PTN (3.5-fold) to M1-UID (2.32-fold) to F5 (1.52-fold), revealing a gradient in the similarity of execution and observation activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C63 quantify a key finding with specific ratios calculated from normalized activity data. The progressive decline across populations (C63) is a clear interpretation supported by the quantitative measurements (C59-C62), consistent with Figure 5 data.

results.result: Population correlations between execution and observation were strong during object cue (r>0.9, p<1×10⁻³²) but diverged during early reach, particularly in M1-PTNs (r=0.15, p=0.2, not significant vs. null distribution). M1-UIDs and F5 remained significantly correlated (p<1×10⁻⁵) though reduced.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C70 present correlation analyses with permutation testing. The temporal dynamics showing divergence specifically during early reach in M1-PTNs (C65, C69-C70) are well-supported by statistical tests and provide key evidence for differential processing across populations.

results.result: F5 showed stronger correlations between object cue and hold periods than M1-PTNs, indicating more consistent activity patterns across these epochs in F5.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 describe cross-temporal pattern analysis results (Figure 6B). The interpretation (C72) follows logically from the observed correlation patterns (C71), supporting functional differences between F5 and M1 in maintaining grasp representations.

results.result: Only F5 showed significant alignment between observation and execution in movement subspace (PG p=0.006, WHG p=0.0007), while M1-PTN and M1-UID alignments were not significantly different from chance (p>0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C74 present PCA subspace analysis with permutation testing. The finding that only F5 shows above-chance alignment is statistically rigorous and represents a central result distinguishing population-level representations across areas.

results.result: Split-trial analysis based on EMG magnitude showed PG M1-PTN alignment was weakly significant for above-median EMG trials (p=0.048) but not below-median trials (p=0.15), suggesting small EMG increases may increase movement subspace capture, particularly in M1-PTN.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 address potential EMG contamination through split-trial analysis. The modest effect (C75) and cautious interpretation (C76) appropriately acknowledge that even small EMG changes can influence alignment measures, strengthening confidence in the main results after EMG exclusion.

results.result: Cross-grasp alignment analysis showed F5 had similar alignment during execution and observation, while both M1 populations showed significantly greater alignment during observation than execution (p<0.01), indicating grasp representations during execution have little bearing on observation representations in M1.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C80 present cross-grasp subspace projections with permutation tests. The finding that M1 shows higher cross-grasp overlap during observation (less grasp-specific) while F5 maintains similar specificity across conditions (C80) is well-supported by the quantitative comparisons (C77-C79).

results.result: Decoding between observation and NoGo conditions was significant at 150 ms in F5 but delayed until 300 ms in M1 populations, suggesting observation and NoGo share more similar initial profiles in M1.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C83 present decoder analysis results (Figure 8C). The temporal difference in decodability (C81-C82) supports the interpretation (C83) that M1 populations initially process observation and NoGo more similarly than F5, consistent with a movement suppression role.

results.result: M1-PTN and M1-UID NoGo activity significantly overlapped with observation activity (M1-PTN: PG p=0.0001, WHG p=0.0001; M1-UID: PG p=0.0007, WHG p=0.0001) with much larger alignment than execution, while execution activity showed no significant overlap.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87 present observation subspace analysis with permutation testing. The strong overlap between NoGo and observation (C84, C86) contrasted with lack of execution overlap (C87) provides compelling evidence that M1 observation activity occupies a 'withholding' subspace.

results.result: F5 showed low overlap between NoGo/execution and observation, though WHG NoGo was significant (p=0.0011).
results.evaluation: Claim C88 completes the observation subspace analysis for F5. The generally low overlap with one exception (WHG NoGo) contrasts with M1 results and supports the interpretation that F5 maintains distinct representations rather than engaging suppression mechanisms.

results.result: F5 maintained similar grasp representations during execution and observation, while M1 population activity during observation was distinct from execution and more closely aligned to NoGo activity, suggesting M1 observation activity contributes to withholding self-movement.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C9 state the primary findings. These are well-supported by the extensive correlation (C64-C70), subspace alignment (C73-C74, C84-C87), and decoding analyses (C81-C83). The interpretation about movement withholding (C9) is reasonable given the NoGo alignment data, though remains inferential.

results.result: M1 and its outputs may dissociate initiation of movement from representation of grasp to flexibly guide behavior.
results.evaluation: Claim C10 is explicitly speculative (marked as SPECULATION in evidence_type). While consistent with the data showing M1 distinguishes execution from observation while F5 maintains grasp representations, this functional interpretation requires additional causal experiments to validate.

results.result: Both F5 and M1 neurons show mirror responses, but F5 mirror activity is more comparable in amplitude to execution (consistent with prior reports), while M1-PTN facilitation-facilitation mirror neurons show 3-4 fold reduction during observation.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 and C94 synthesize current findings with prior literature. The amplitude comparisons are supported by Figure 4-5 data and quantitative measurements (C59-C62), and consistency with previous reports (Dushanova and Donoghue 2010; Vigneswaran et al. 2013) strengthens confidence.

results.result: M1-PTN mirror neurons showed particularly weak correlation during early movement and movement execution subspaces captured meaningful observation variance in F5 but not M1 populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C96 summarize key correlation (Figure 6A) and PCA (Figure 7) results. These are directly supported by the statistical analyses in C65, C69-C70, C73-C74 and represent core findings distinguishing population dynamics.

results.result: During observation, grasp selectivity is similar in F5 but markedly reduced in M1.
results.evaluation: Claim C97 interprets the cross-grasp alignment results (C77-C79). The higher cross-grasp overlap during observation in M1 (indicating reduced selectivity) is well-supported by the permutation test results showing significantly greater alignment during observation than execution.

results.result: M1 activity during execution and observation, particularly in PTNs, may be sufficiently dissimilar to ensure movement is only produced during execution.
results.evaluation: Claim C99 synthesizes multiple findings (correlation, subspace, decoding analyses) into a functional interpretation. While inferential, this is well-supported by the extensive evidence of dissimilarity between execution and observation in M1-PTNs (C65, C69-C70, C73-C74, C95-C96).

results.result: The UID population reflects a mixed population of interneurons and pyramidal cells, possibly including unidentified PTNs, and spike width-based classification is unreliable in non-human primates.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 acknowledge limitations in UID classification. C100 is supported by citation (Soteropoulos 2018) and C101 by citation (Vigneswaran et al. 2011). This appropriately qualifies interpretation of UID results and explains why PTN-UID differences were not always clear.

results.result: Correlations between execution and observation began decreasing during late reaction period before movement, and single-neuron firing rates showed little correlation with movement speed.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103 address potential confounds from movement timing differences. C102 is supported by Figure 6A showing divergence before movement onset, and C103 rules out speed encoding as an explanation, strengthening the interpretation that differences reflect processing distinctions rather than kinematic factors.

results.result: The dissociation between execution and observation appeared most prominent in the lead up to movement onset, consistent with previous suggestions about mirror neuron roles in movement suppression.
results.evaluation: Claim C106 summarizes temporal dynamics with citations to prior work (Kraskov et al. 2009; Vigneswaran et al. 2013). This is supported by correlation analyses (C64-C70) showing divergence during early reach and is consistent with the broader literature on mirror neuron function.

results.result: While M1 prioritizes distinguishing movement from non-movement from an egocentric perspective, F5 maintains more similar representations across executed and observed actions, independent of acting agent identity.
results.evaluation: Claim C111 provides a high-level functional interpretation of the findings. This is well-supported by the totality of evidence showing F5 maintains similar execution-observation representations (C6, C73, C77, C90) while M1 distinguishes them (C7, C65, C74, C78-C79), though the interpretation remains inferential.

results.result: The pseudo-randomized trial sequence and simultaneous provision of Go/NoGo and execution/observation information ensured equivalent timing of movement cues across conditions and prevented anticipation.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 describe critical task design features. These are methodological facts that strengthen the study by ensuring conditions were matched in timing and unpredictability, reducing potential confounds in comparing neural responses across conditions.

results.result: PTNs in F5 and M1 provide direct spinal input, are critical for skilled movement, and contrary to initial hypotheses, can be active during action observation without movement.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 state established anatomical/functional knowledge, while C3 presents a key finding validated by the current data (EMG controls C35, C39) and prior work. This frames the central question of how observation activity is prevented from producing movement.

results.result: Mirror neurons are embedded in a parieto-frontal network integral to visually-guided grasp, with activity during observation occurring without detectable movement despite PTN involvement. Prior work suggests movement-related activity unfolds in orthogonal dimensions to preparation, with similar mechanisms hypothesized for observation and suppression.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C31 provide comprehensive literature review establishing the context and prior findings. All are appropriately cited and accurately represent the state of knowledge, including the dynamical systems framework (C26-C29) and prior state-space analyses (C30-C31) that motivate the current approach.

results.result: F5 makes limited contribution to the corticospinal tract but is anatomically and functionally strongly interconnected with M1.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 state established anatomical facts with appropriate citations. This contextualizes why F5 and M1 might show different relationships between execution and observation activity given their differential contributions to direct motor output.

results.result: M1 was initially thought to lack mirror neurons, but subsequent studies showed M1 neurons including PTNs can show mirror responses, though activity is often relatively weak.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 accurately summarize the evolution of understanding about M1 mirror neurons with appropriate citations. This historical context frames the current findings about weak M1 observation activity relative to execution.

results.result: The finding that execution and observation patterns are more similar in F5 than M1 is consistent with recent work showing premotor but not M1 mirror neurons recapitulate execution state transitions during observation.
results.evaluation: Claim C98 appropriately connects current findings to recent complementary work (Mazurek et al. 2018). The consistency across studies using different analytical approaches strengthens confidence in the conclusion about differential processing in premotor vs. motor cortex.

results.result: Cells in dorsal premotor areas and proximal M1 representations mirror reaching movements and are key to generating reaching actions.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C105 cite relevant literature on reaching-related mirror neurons. This addresses the potential concern that the focus on grasp-related areas might limit generalizability, noting that mirror properties extend to reaching representations.

results.result: Observed actions in peri-personal space modulate mirror neuron responses differently than actions beyond reach, suggesting the capability to interact with observed actions contributes to mirror activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C110 cite relevant prior work and draw a reasonable inference about how task context (peri-personal space) may have influenced results. This appropriately qualifies the findings and suggests boundary conditions for the observed effects.

results.result: Experiments used two adult male rhesus macaques (M48: 12.0 kg, M49: 10.5 kg) with all procedures approved by UCL Animal Welfare and Ethical Review Body under UK Home Office licenses. Animals were euthanized at study end.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C114 provide required methodological and ethical information. These are factual statements about subjects and procedures that are appropriately documented.
